prompt: Why does the lesson say there is no best tool?
hint: Best for what, for whom, and at what cost of leaving?

choices.text: Benchmarks are rigged by the vendors who publish them
choices.why: Benchmarks may be fair and still answer a question your system is not asking.

choices.text: A tool fits a set of quality attributes, a team and an exit cost
choices.why: Right: fit is relative to those three, so the same tool is right in one place and wrong in another.

choices.text: Every tool becomes obsolete within a few years
choices.why: Age is not the argument; PostgreSQL won Tracking's decision and it is decades old.

choices.text: Architects should leave tool choices to vendors
choices.why: The lesson gives the team six questions to decide with; nobody hands it to a vendor.

prompt: A fleet of 4,500 trucks reports a GPS position every 30 seconds at the busiest hour. How many positions a second does Tracking receive?
hint: Trucks divided by the interval in seconds.

prompt: All three candidates for Tracking's position store could carry 100 writes a second. What decided between them?
hint: When fit does not separate the options, the other five questions do.

choices.text: The newest option, since it will age best
choices.why: Novelty was not one of the six questions, and the oldest option won.

choices.text: A benchmark at ten times the current load
choices.why: Ten times the fleet is when to look again, not what decided this time.

choices.text: The enthusiasm of the engineer who had used the dedicated database
choices.why: He was right about its strengths and was the only one who could run it, which counted against it.

choices.text: Team skill, operating cost and exit cost
choices.why: Right: the team could run PostgreSQL, it added nothing to on-call, and it was the cheapest to leave.

prompt: The lesson calls team skill "a quality attribute in disguise". Which quality attribute, in the Tracking example?
hint: Think of three in the morning and one person's holidays.

choices.text: Availability
choices.why: Right: a database that one person knows how to debug stays down while that person is away.

choices.text: Throughput, because the team writes slower code in an unfamiliar tool
choices.why: The load was modest for every candidate; speed of writing code was not the risk.

choices.text: Security of the stored positions
choices.why: Nothing in the example ties skill to security.

choices.text: Portability across cloud providers
choices.why: That belongs to the exit question, which is a separate one.

prompt: In Bezos's terms, what is a two-way door?
hint: If it turns out badly, what do you do?

choices.text: A decision two teams take together
choices.why: Who decides is the second axis the lesson adds, not what the door means.

choices.text: A decision that needs a record and a review
choices.why: That is the treatment a one-way door earns.

choices.text: One you walk back through and change cheaply
choices.why: Right: reversible, so it deserves a light, fast process.

choices.text: One whose consequences are both good and bad
choices.why: Every decision has both; the door is about reversibility.

prompt: Which of these turn a one-way door into a more two-way one, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Most of the cost of reversing is the code that knows about the choice.

choices.text: Putting the technology behind an interface your code owns
choices.why: Yes: the knowledge of the tool stays in one place.

choices.text: Versioning a public contract from its first release
choices.why: Yes: a second version can live beside the first.

choices.text: Choosing the option with the most stars on its repository
choices.why: Popularity says nothing about the cost of leaving.

choices.text: Deciding faster, so the door is behind you sooner
choices.why: Speed through a one-way door makes it no more reversible.

prompt: Which part of Nygard's record holds the forces at play: what is true and what pulls each way?
hint: It comes before the decision.

choices.text: Consequences
choices.why: Those say what becomes true after the decision.

choices.text: Context
choices.why: Right: the situation the decision answers.

choices.text: Status
choices.why: Status records where the record is in its life.

choices.text: Title
choices.why: The title names the decision in a short phrase.

prompt: Record 7's context says "Payments must not read Tracking's database". Why is that a good line for a context?
hint: What does a good force do to the options?

choices.text: It sounds firm, which discourages objections in the review
choices.why: A record is reviewed to find objections early, not to discourage them.

choices.text: It names the person responsible for the database
choices.why: It names a constraint, not a person.

choices.text: It is checkable and rules an option out
choices.why: Right: a reader verifies it and sees what it excludes, unlike "a robust, decoupled design".

choices.text: Every context in Carreto's template begins with an ownership rule
choices.why: No such template rule appears in the lesson.

prompt: Why does record 7 list the extra work Payments takes on, such as handling duplicate events and running a nightly check?
hint: A record that lists only benefits reads like what?

choices.text: To justify a larger budget for Payments
choices.why: Budgets are not the record's purpose.

choices.text: Costs are consequences too
choices.why: Right: a reader who finds the costs alone stops trusting the rest of the log.

choices.text: So that Tracking's team feels responsible for them
choices.why: The costs land on Payments, and naming them is for every future reader.

choices.text: Because Nygard's format requires a separate risk section
choices.why: The format has no risk section; costs belong in consequences.

prompt: Put the parts of Nygard's record in the order they appear.
hint: The decision needs its context first, and its consequences after.
trap: Putting the decision before the context makes a reader judge it without the forces that justified it.

prompt: A year after record 7 was accepted, Payments shortens the contest window and the decision itself changes. What happens to record 7?
hint: Only one line of an accepted record is edited.

choices.text: Its decision and consequences are updated to match the new design
choices.why: Editing an accepted record erases why the old decision was right at the time.

choices.text: It is deleted, since the code no longer matches it
choices.why: Deleting it loses the history the log exists to keep.

choices.text: A new record supersedes it, and its status points there
choices.why: Right: the old text stays; the status line is the one edit.

choices.text: It is marked deprecated, with no successor
choices.why: Deprecated is for a decision that stops applying with nothing in its place.

prompt: Match each status to its meaning.
hint: Four statuses, one life.

pairs.right: committed to, and its text now fixed
no longer applies, nothing replaced it

prompt: A new engineer wants to delete Payments' nightly check because it has found nothing in weeks. What does record 7 tell her that the code does not?
hint: Chesterton's fence.

choices.text: Who wrote the job, so she can ask him
choices.why: The record names a decision and its reasons; the author may have left.

choices.text: That it is the way a lost event gets noticed
choices.why: Right: finding nothing is the job working; the night it finds something, a driver gets paid.

choices.text: How the job is scheduled and which API it calls
choices.why: That is what the code already shows.

choices.text: That deleting jobs requires the architect's approval
choices.why: No such rule exists; the record gives a reason, not a permission.

prompt: Kátia proposes polling again for a different integration, and Renata points at record 7. What question does the lesson say the conversation turns on?
hint: Revisiting starts from somewhere specific.

choices.text: Who decided last time, and do they still agree?
choices.why: Who decided matters less than whether the forces have moved.

choices.text: Is polling simpler than events?
choices.why: It is simpler, and record 7 already weighed that.

choices.text: What in the context has changed?
choices.why: Right: if nothing, the decision stands; if something, a new record supersedes it.

choices.text: Does Renata have authority to refuse it?
choices.why: The record moves the talk from authority to forces.

prompt: A forum of 6 people spends 1 hour on an already settled question, 4 times a year, for 2 years. How many engineer-hours does that cost?
hint: People times hours times meetings a year times years.

prompt: Record 7's event approach causes an incident a year later, when the broker loses messages in an unforeseen way. How does the record help the review that follows?
hint: Judged by what was known, not by what happened.

choices.text: It proves that events were the wrong choice
choices.why: An outcome after the fact does not show the decision was wrong with what was known then.

choices.text: It identifies who to hold responsible
choices.why: The useful review asks whether the safeguard worked, not who chose events.

choices.text: It shows the incident could not have been prevented
choices.why: The record shows what was foreseen; it makes no claim about what was preventable.

choices.text: It shows lost events were foreseen and a check was built for them
choices.why: Right: the review asks whether the nightly check worked, instead of rewriting history with hindsight.

prompt: Which of these decisions deserve a record, by the lesson's test? Choose all that apply.
hint: One-way doors, and decisions reaching beyond one team.

choices.text: Pricing switching logging library
choices.why: A two-way door inside one team.

choices.text: Tracking storing a year of positions in PostgreSQL
choices.why: Yes: one team, but expensive to reverse.

choices.text: The fields of the DeliveryProved event
choices.why: Yes: a contract between two teams.

choices.text: Renaming a private module inside Payments
choices.why: Cheap to undo and invisible outside the team.

prompt: A team writes its records after each change has merged, filling in the template from the pull request. What does the lesson predict?
hint: Paperwork after the fact.

choices.text: Contexts argue for what was built, and readers learn the log is decoration
choices.why: Right: rejected options get invented to look fair, and nobody trusts the log.

choices.text: Records get better, because the final design is known
choices.why: Knowing the result is exactly what bends the context towards it.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the content is the same
choices.why: Timing changes the content: the review that could have caught an objection never happened.

choices.text: Reviews get slower, because pull requests carry more files
choices.why: The lesson's worry is trust in the log, not review speed.

prompt: When a decision changes, its record is not edited: a new record ___ it.
hint: The status that points at a successor.

prompt: Carreto's public API, which shippers' own systems call, needs a breaking change. Where does it sit on the lesson's two axes, and what follows?
hint: Outside parties whose projects Carreto cannot schedule.

choices.text: Bottom left: one team owns the API, so it decides quickly
choices.why: One team writes it, but the reach is outside the company.

choices.text: Bottom right: agree the contract with one shipper and ship
choices.why: Reversing is expensive here, because every integration has to move.

choices.text: Top right: a one-way door
choices.why: Right: far-reaching and costly to undo, so it gets a record and a new version beside the old one.

choices.text: Top left: expensive, but inside one team
choices.why: The cost lands on outside companies, not inside one team.

prompt: Match each of the six questions to what it asks of a candidate technology.
hint: Fit, skill, ecosystem, licence, cost, exit.

pairs.right: can this team debug it at three in the morning?
what may we do with it, and can that change?
what would leaving cost in three years?
is it documented, supported, and can we hire for it?

right_distractors: does it have the most stars on its repository?

prompt: Renata did not write record 7. What was her part, by the lesson?
hint: Exists, reviewed, findable.

choices.text: Approving it before Bruno was allowed to merge
choices.why: The lesson gives her no approval gate; that would be a bottleneck.

choices.text: Making sure it existed, was reviewed and could be found
choices.why: Right: and asking who writes it and by when.

choices.text: Rewriting it in her own words for consistency
choices.why: Records written by the teams teach the teams to think in decisions.

choices.text: Choosing the event option herself and informing the teams
choices.why: The teams decided after the working session; she asked the questions.
